newsitem.title: UK: Two drugs good for AIDS, but three better -- studies.
newsitem.headline: Two drugs good for AIDS, but three better -- studies.

text.p: A combination of two drugs works well against the HIV virus that causes AIDS but three are better, researchers reported on Monday.
Adding new types of drugs to the cocktail greatly increases the effects, the doctors told the Third International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection, being held in Birmingham.
The reports add to a growing body of evidence that the earlier and harder the virus is hit, the easier it is to suppress it.
Glaxo Wellcome Plc reported that dual therapy using its Epivir (3TC) and Retrovir (AZT) cut deaths from AIDS by more than 50 percent.

Data from the CAESAR trial of nearly 1,900 patients in 14 countries showed the best results yet from this class of drug, known as nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, the company told the 1,700 delegates at the congress.
Epivir plus AZT reduced the progression of HIV infection to full-blown AIDS or death by 54 percent, and to death alone by 53 percent.
But other reports showed that adding either protease inhibitors or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors worked even better.
These drugs attack the HIV virus at a different point in its cycle of replication and doctors are finding that the more ways they attack HIV, the less the chance it can mutate to thwart them.
Cassy Workman and colleagues at the University of New South Wales in Sydney reported on five patients given either AZT plus 3TC or AZT, 3TC and Hoffman-La Roche's saquinavir, a protease inhibitor.
All the patients got better, but saquinavir had dramatic effects, the researchers told the conference. The virus was suppressed to below detectable levels in those who took saquinavir.
But they added a warning -- the drugs are new and no patient has taken protease inhibitors for more than two years.
"It remains to be determined if this reduction in viral load is sustainable and results in an improved, disease-free period," they said.
Some of the researchers found that protease inhibitors were not necessarily needed to give a triple cocktail a good punch.

Researchers at Montreal's McGill University AIDS centre studied the effects of AZT and Bristol-Myers Squibb's ddI (correct: ddI) combined with Boehringer Ingelheim's nevirapine (Viramune), which belongs to another new class of drugs known as non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
"The use of triple drug therapy has led to non-detectable levels of virus in plasma (blood) in over 75 percent of patients who were previously drug-naive (had not been given any drugs)," they said.
Joep Lange and colleagues at Amsterdam's Academic Medical Centre, working with Boehringer, found similar results.
"The triple therapy was clearly superior by 12 months," they reported. "Nevirapine provides new opportunities for combination treatment."

But some researchers warned against a third drug being added to an existing regime. Ian Weller of University College London said that if patients were not responding to a two-drug combination they should be put on three completely new drugs to avoid the risk of the virus developing a drug resistance.
